primary_topics: Address at a US-ASEAN Business Council forum, March 30, 2011 -- invited by Washington Sycip, SGV Chairman Cirilo Noel and AIM President Edilberto De Jesus; addressed to US business representatives assessing the investment climate under President Aquino
Three complaints against the judiciary: corruption, incompetence and delay (CID) -- illustrated by the fictional Judge Cerapio I. Delayo and the Mercedes Benz bribery joke
The right solution: not constitutional change, not new laws, but changing the officials -- 'a change from the inside out, a change of hearts, a change of values, a change in ethical backbone'

CJP's APJR legacy: established the Philippine Judicial Academy with P300 million Japanese grant; Mandatory Continuing Legal Education; filled vacant judgeships; computerization with World Bank/USAID/CIDA/EU support; World Bank cited APJR as its global model; APJR abandoned after 2006 and taken off the World Bank website
sub_topics: Judge CID joke: lawyer visits judge at home; judge: 'Why are you here? Don't you know it is unethical to talk with a judge about a pending case outside the courtroom?'; lawyer: 'I did not come to speak about my case. But if you will look outside your window, you will see a sparkling new Mercedes Benz S560'; judge: 'That is worse; you have come to bribe me!'; lawyer: 'I am not giving you the car. I am selling it to you'; judge: 'How much?'; lawyer: 'Fifty dollars'; judge: 'In that case, I will buy two!' -- illustrates all three CID complaints

Wrong solution 1 -- constitutional change: 'I believe that the presidential system, which we borrowed from the United States and improved upon based on lessons learned from the Marcos years, is not the source of our problems. The US Constitution does not provide for an independent Commission on Election, yet elections in America are generally peaceful and orderly.'

Wrong solution 2 -- new laws: 'I also believe the second proposal, to pass new laws to increase judicial salaries and combat corruption, is also not the priority. During my incumbency in the Supreme Court, the legislature already doubled judicial compensations. We have enough laws to punish crimes.'

The right solution: 'It is changing the officials who subvert our institutions and make a mockery of our laws... not just a change of leaders, but a change in our leaders... A change from the inside out, a change of hearts, a change of values, a change in ethical backbone.'

APJR achievements: Philippine Judicial Academy (P300 million JICA grant; buildings in Tagaytay City); Mandatory Continuing Legal Education (MCLE -- retraining for all lawyers every three years); filled vacant judgeships nationwide; computerization program with World Bank, USAID, CIDA and EU support

APJR recognition and abandonment: 'I am proud to tell you that our APJR was cited by the World Bank as its official model in assisting other judiciaries in the world. Unfortunately, after I retired in 2006, the Court gave little priority to the Action Program for Judicial Reform. Sadly, the APJR was taken off the World Bank's website as a model judicial reform program.'

Judicial philosophy: strict scrutiny for civil liberties (scales weigh against government, favor the people, especially the poor); deferential interpretation for prosperity and economic conflicts (defer to political branches)

Investment call: 'the Philippines should be experiencing a renaissance in the near future... I hope you will find renewed trust in our economy and will be the first to place your investments in the new Philippines. Join the battle cry of President Noynoy Aquino, Kung Walang Corrupt, Walang Mahirap.'

stances.claim: The APJR's removal from the World Bank's website after CJP's retirement is the most concrete institutional failure of the post-Panganiban Court. A judicial reform program so successful that the World Bank used it as a global model -- and which received support from the World Bank, USAID, CIDA and EU -- was quietly abandoned, and the international support dried up accordingly.
stances.rhetorical_move: institutional-abandonment-as-tragedy: the APJR's World Bank deletion as the most measurable evidence of what the judiciary lost after CJP's retirement
stances.confidence: asserted as a documented institutional fact

stances.claim: Constitutional change and new laws are the wrong solutions to judicial corruption, incompetence and delay. The presidential system works fine (as proven by the US, which does not even have an independent Comelec but has peaceful elections); and enough laws already exist to punish corruption. The problem is not the system but the people running it -- requiring a change of hearts, values and ethical backbone.
stances.rhetorical_move: system-is-not-the-problem argument: the US Constitution analogy (no independent Comelec, yet peaceful elections) as proof that the Philippine system is structurally sound and only needs ethical leaders

notable_anecdotes: Judge CID buys two Mercedes: the Mercedes Benz S560 at $50 joke -- when the lawyer reveals he is 'selling it' at that price, Judge CID says 'In that case, I will buy two!' -- a corruption joke that also illustrates incompetence (he can't see the problem) and delay (he's trying to manage the case).

P300 million JICA grant for PJA: 'As Chief Justice, I was able to obtain from the Japanese government a grant of P300 million, which was used to construct the Academy's buildings in Tagaytay City.' -- a specific achievement not mentioned in other batch entries.

APJR World Bank deletion: 'APJR was cited by the World Bank as its official model in assisting other judiciaries in the world. Unfortunately, after I retired in 2006, the Court gave little priority to the APJR. Sadly, the APJR was taken off the World Bank's website as a model judicial reform program.' -- the most poignant institutional loss in the corpus.

Change-of-hearts as the right solution: 'not just a change of leaders, but a change in our leaders... a change from the inside out, a change of hearts, a change of values, a change in ethical backbone' -- the governing conviction that institutions are only as good as the people who run them.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered March 30, 2011 at a US-ASEAN Business Council forum -- invited by Washington Sycip (SGV founder), Cirilo Noel (SGV Chairman) and Edilberto De Jesus (AIM President), with Council President Alexander C. Feldman flying from Washington DC to assess the Philippine investment climate under President Aquino -- this address by CJP begins with the fictional Judge Cerapio I. Delayo (CID) and the Mercedes Benz S560 joke (lawyer: 'I'm selling it for fifty dollars'; judge: 'In that case, I will buy two!') to illustrate the three most common judicial complaints: Corruption, Incompetence and Delay. He rejects constitutional change (the presidential system is fine -- the US has peaceful elections without an independent Comelec) and new salary laws (the legislature already doubled judicial compensations during his term; enough laws exist to punish crimes). The right solution: 'not just a change of leaders, but a change in our leaders... a change from the inside out, a change of hearts, a change of values, a change in ethical backbone.' During his incumbency, the APJR achieved: the Philippine Judicial Academy (P300 million JICA grant; buildings in Tagaytay City); Mandatory Continuing Legal Education (all lawyers retrained every three years); filled vacant judgeships; computerization program (World Bank, USAID, CIDA, EU). 'I am proud to tell you that our APJR was cited by the World Bank as its official model in assisting other judiciaries in the world. Unfortunately, after I retired in 2006, the Court gave little priority to the APJR. Sadly, the APJR was taken off the World Bank's website as a model judicial reform program.' He restates his judicial philosophy (strict scrutiny for civil liberties; deferential interpretation for economic matters) and closes with an investment invitation: 'Join the battle cry of President Noynoy Aquino, Kung Walang Corrupt, Walang Mahirap.'
